name: Squalene
lead: Squalene is an oily hydrocarbon (C30H50) and an intermediate in the biosynthesis of sterols such as cholesterol. It takes its name from Squalus, the shark genus whose liver oil was its first major source, and it is also made by the human body and secreted in skin sebum, where it forms part of the skin's surface lipids.[1][2][6]

In personal care it is used as a lightweight emollient and lubricant in moisturisers and facial oils, where it is meant to soften the skin and leave a smooth, non-greasy feel. Its presence in human sebum is the usual rationale for describing it as skin-compatible. A hydrogenated, more oxidation-stable relative called squalane is the form more commonly seen in cosmetic ingredient lists. Sources include shark liver oil, olive oil, amaranth oil, plus synthetic and microbial production.[1][2][7] Squalene is also an ingredient of oil-in-water emulsion adjuvants used in some vaccines.[1]

Toxicology reviews summarised by Wikipedia indicate low acute toxicity and little contact allergy at cosmetic concentrations.[1] A 2023 safety assessment of squalane and squalene in the International Journal of Toxicology covers their use in cosmetics.[7] No published human trial was found testing squalene by itself for an appearance outcome such as acne, wrinkles or skin texture.

paras: Squalene is a colourless to yellowish oil made of six isoprene units linked tail to tail, with six double bonds that give it its chemical reactivity toward oxidants.[1][2] Most plants, fungi and animals make it by joining two molecules of farnesyl pyrophosphate in a reaction catalysed by squalene synthase, the first step committed to sterol production.[1][2]

It is then oxidised by squalene epoxidase to 2,3-oxidosqualene, cyclised to lanosterol and converted onward to sterols including cholesterol, which in turn is the precursor to bile acids, vitamin D and steroid hormones.[2] Because the double bonds make squalene prone to oxidation, the saturated derivative squalane, produced by hydrogenation, is used where shelf stability matters; Wikipedia notes that squalane is a distinct compound from squalene.[1]

The Japanese researcher Mitsumaru Tsujimoto reported an unsaponifiable fraction in deep-sea shark liver oil in 1906 and established the formula C30H50 in 1916. Paul Karrer and A. Helfenstein synthesised it in 1931.[1]

Deep-water shark liver oil, from sharks living at around 500 metres and deeper, is the richest natural source, at roughly 50 to 80 percent. Amaranth oil (about 1 to 7 percent) has the highest plant content, olive oil carries about 0.2 to 0.5 percent, and the deodorised distillate of olive oil is a concentrated source. Synthetic production from geranylacetone and engineered microbes are further routes.[1] In 2020 conservation groups raised concern that vaccine demand for squalene could lead to shark killing, a concern that has encouraged extraction from other sources.[1]

Squalene is a component of human sebum; Wikipedia gives an estimate that about 12 percent of the body's squalene is found there.[1] Studies of human stratum corneum lipids have characterised the lipid composition of the skin surface, which is the background for describing squalene as skin-identical.[8] This origin is the usual rationale for its use as a lightweight emollient in moisturisers and oils.[1][2]

Grokipedia describes it as compatible with skin lipids and as an antioxidant-like ingredient because of its many double bonds, though it also notes that it can react with oxidants.[2] Cosmetic formulation research on nano-emulsions, which are used to carry oils like squalene in personal care products, discusses their advantages over larger-droplet emulsions.[9]

Toxicology studies summarised on Wikipedia indicate low acute toxicity and little irritation or contact allergy at cosmetic concentrations.[1] The International Journal of Toxicology published a 2023 safety assessment covering squalane and squalene in cosmetic use.[7]

Vaccine use is a separate topic: the WHO is reported to have recorded no significant vaccine-related adverse events among over 22 million doses of a squalene-adjuvanted influenza vaccine used in Europe since 1997, and a 2009 meta-analysis of 64 trials reported no increase in autoimmune disease with MF59-adjuvanted vaccines.[1] Gulf War syndrome claims have been reviewed and the vaccines concerned are reported not to have contained squalene.[1] A 2002 randomised trial measured antibodies to squalene in anthrax vaccine recipients.[10]

Squalene appears in nutrition discussions as a minor constituent of olive oil, rice bran oil and amaranth. In T Nation forum threads, members list it among the beneficial compounds of olive oil, olives and rice bran oil.[11][12] Forum members have also discussed squalene as a vaccine adjuvant, with some saying they would avoid squalene-containing vaccines.[13][14]

A homeopathic-labelled oral product listed on DailyMed includes squalene among many ingredients; its label says the statements are based on homeopathic principles and have not been reviewed by the FDA.[15]

Squalene accumulation has been studied in cell biology, including a 2019 Nature paper on cholesterol-auxotrophic lymphoma cells, and squalene derivatives are covered in recurring natural product reviews of triterpenoids.[16][17] These lines of work concern metabolism rather than skin appearance.

No studies found for squalene as a topical appearance treatment. Squalene-based emulsion adjuvants have been tested in many vaccine trials (for example AS03 or MF59 adjuvanted influenza vaccines), which concern immune response rather than skin.[3][4] A 2024 randomised trial in Scientific Reports gave a sublingual squalene microemulsion extracted from pumpkin seed oil to hospitalised COVID-19 patients, with 301 patients in each of two groups, and examined mortality.[18] A registered study of skin hydration measurement (NCT05071456) lists atopic dermatitis and acne as conditions but its relevance to squalene is not established.[5]

lore.intro: Squalene comes up on T Nation mainly in two contexts: as a dietary compound in olive oil and other oils, and as a vaccine adjuvant.[11][13]

claims.claim: Squalene in olive oil is a 'heart-healthy compound'.
claims.believers: A T Nation post listing top foods describes olive oil as containing a heart-healthy compound called squalene alongside its monounsaturated fat.[11]
claims.experts: Wikipedia gives olive oil's squalene content as about 0.2 to 0.5 percent; no trial in the sources tested dietary squalene for appearance outcomes.[1]

claims.believers: Forum members in 2009 threads said they would not accept squalene-adjuvanted vaccines.[13][14]
claims.experts: The WHO is reported to have recorded no significant vaccine-related adverse events among over 22 million squalene-adjuvanted flu vaccine doses, and a 2009 meta-analysis of 64 trials found no increase in autoimmune disease.[1]

claims.claim: Squalene is skin-identical, so applying it supports skin.
claims.believers: Skincare descriptions cite its presence in human sebum as the reason it blends with the skin's lipids.[2]
claims.experts: Toxicology reviews report low irritation at cosmetic concentrations;[1][7] no human trial was found testing squalene alone for acne, wrinkles or texture.

card.summary: A skin-identical oil used as a lightweight emollient; safe-looking but with no trials for appearance outcomes.
card.aka: Shark-derived or olive-derived squalene; squalane is its hydrogenated form
card.note: Also used in vaccine adjuvants; that research is unrelated to skin outcomes.

quick.overview:
Squalene is a natural oil that the body makes and that appears in skin sebum. In skincare it is used as a light emollient, sourced from shark liver, olive or amaranth oil, or made synthetically.

Its appearance benefits are described mostly in terms of its skin-like origin; no published human trial was found testing it for acne, ageing or texture.
quick.mechanism: It is an emollient that sits on and blends with the skin's lipid layer. In the body it is a step in making cholesterol.
quick.risks: Reviews summarised by Wikipedia report low toxicity and little allergy at cosmetic levels. Its many double bonds mean it can oxidise. Shark sourcing has been a conservation concern.

chain: Applied as an oil or as part of a moisturiser
Adds a skin-compatible lipid layer that softens the surface
angle.text: Squalene is applied topically as an emollient, so its effect on looks is at the surface: it lubricates and softens skin and helps products spread. Users typically choose it, or its hydrogenated form squalane, for a light feel that resembles the skin's own oils.
